deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no derivation. It is page IV of the printed 'Vorbericht' (preface) of an arithmetic and algebra textbook. The bundle name 'HB.Leiste' suggests Christian Leiste's 'Die Arithmetik und Algebra' (Wolfenbüttel, 1790), probably a copy from Gauss's library or one associated with him; this attribution is likely but not certain. There is no handwriting by Gauss visible on the page, only a faint library stamp at the bottom.

The author makes four points about teaching.
(1) A textbook should keep some propositions in reserve, unsolved, for the curiosity and diligence of brighter students. The teacher can then help individually, and this can awaken everyone's interest. Once interest is awakened, every proposition can be made clear even to average students.
(2) The book aims to give the reasons behind all the arithmetic of everyday commercial life, with enough examples to understand and explain any properly written 'Rechenbuch'.
(3) Method:
- Letter-algebra ('Buchstaben-Rechnung') is introduced from the start alongside ordinary numerals.
- Everything is built on the concept of ratio ('Verhältnis'). The general expression of a number in §21 is chosen so that all operations with integers and fractions follow from it. This is presumably a number viewed as a ratio to a unit, in the spirit of Newton's definition in Arithmetica Universalis; this reading is mine and inferred, since §21 is not on this page.
- The author claims simpler treatments of division of fractions and of the 'verkehrte Regel de tri' (inverse rule of three, i.e., inverse proportion: a1·b1 = a2·b2, so x = a·b/c).
(4) The page transitions to a short history of the science, which continues on the next page.

The only mathematical content is implicit and elementary:
- Division of fractions: (a/b)/(c/d) = a·d/(b·c).
- Inverse rule of three: if quantity a corresponds to b under inverse proportion, then c corresponds to a·b/c.
